prompt: A member country can produce a good at $90, a non-member at $70, and the external tariff is $30. After customs-union formation, from whom will the importing country buy?

prompt: Before a customs union, domestic production costs $140, a member supplier costs $100 and a non-member costs $80. A $70 tariff applies to both imports, so domestic output is produced. After union formation, member imports are tariff-free while the non-member still faces the tariff. What occurs?

options.label: A
options.text: Trade creation from costly domestic output to cheaper member imports

options.label: B
options.text: Trade diversion from previously cheapest non-member imports to member imports

options.label: C
options.text: No change because domestic output remains the cheapest source

options.label: D
options.text: Monetary integration because a shared currency replaces tariff preferences

explanation: Before integration, member imports cost $170 and non-member imports cost $150 including the $70 tariff, so domestic production at $140 is cheapest. Removing the member tariff makes member imports at $100 replace domestic production. This is trade creation, although the non-member resource cost of $80 remains lower.
reference: 11.6 Globalisation | 11.6.3 trade creation and trade diversion | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: Domestic production costs $140, a member supplier costs $100 and a non-member costs $80. A $70 external tariff makes domestic production cheapest before union formation. After the member tariff is removed, the country switches to member imports. Why can this still improve welfare?

options.label: A
options.text: Any supplier charging more than the world’s lowest resource cost makes welfare gains impossible

options.label: B
options.text: Member imports save resources versus previous domestic output

options.label: C
options.text: Tariff revenue necessarily increases when member imports become duty free

options.label: D
options.text: Tariff removal cannot cut prices

explanation: The tariff-free member supply saves $40 of resources per unit relative to the former $140 domestic source. The outside supplier would save even more resources at $80, but that does not remove the real improvement from replacing domestic output with $100 member imports. Consumption gains may also arise from the lower price.
reference: 11.6 Globalisation | 11.6.3 trade creation and trade diversion | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: A member supplier costs $95, a non-member costs $70 and the common external tariff is $35. Before union formation the country imports from the non-member at $105 including tariff. After joining, it imports from the member at $95. Which welfare concern is central?

options.label: A

options.label: B
options.text: Only expensive domestic production is replaced by imports

options.label: C
options.text: Tariff receipts disappear while imports use costlier resources

options.label: D
options.text: The external tariff has no influence on sourcing

prompt: A customs union lowers the domestic price from 120 to 100. Consumer-surplus gains are 50, producer-surplus losses are 20 and tariff revenue falls by 40. What is the net domestic welfare change?

options.label: B
options.text: A gain of 30

options.label: C
options.text: A loss of 10

prompt: A customs union lowers the domestic price. Consumer-surplus gain is 80, producer-surplus loss is 35 and tariff-revenue loss is 25. What is the net domestic welfare change?

options.text: A loss of 20

options.label: C
options.text: A gain of 20

options.label: D
